ctx-rain.prompt: A neighbourhood association holds a big picnic once a year in the name of “development”; the picnic contributes nothing to development. Which of the following is a functionalist question?
options: What do people say to each other at the picnic, and what meaning do they give the phrase “our neighbourhood”?
Even if the picnic does not reach its stated aim, does it bring members together and strengthen the group’s bond?
Is the picnic permitted and legal?
How should a survey measuring how happy participants are at the end of the picnic be designed?
ctx-rain.explain: The functionalist question probes a practice through its contribution to the whole (here, the neighbourhood), regardless of its stated aim; that is exactly the move in Merton’s rain-ceremony example. The first option asks how meaning is built, so it is interactionist. The third is a legal question and the fourth a measurement question; neither asks about a practice’s social consequences.

ctx-why-media.prompt: A researcher asks hundreds of people for long written answers, in their own words, to “what did you experience with the cinema?”. Which view does this choice sit closer to?
options: Functionalist: because it measures the job the cinema does for society.
Interactionist: because it tries to capture meaning through people’s own accounts.
Functionalist: because a written answer is always objective data.
Neither: written accounts do not count as scientific data.
ctx-why-media.explain: Having people narrate in their own words rests on capturing meaning from the actor’s point of view, which is the distinctive move of the interactionist view. The first and third options tie the method to the wrong view: the functionalist question asks “what job does it do for society?”, and a written account speaks of meaning, not of that. The last option is wrong too: such accounts are legitimate data in qualitative research; they are just not suited to exact counting.

people-cast.prompt: Match the names with their best-remembered contributions.
pairs: Everyday life in the language of the stage
people-cast.explain: The pairs most often confused are Cooley and Mead (the looking-glass self is Cooley’s; the “I”, the “me” and the generalized other are Mead’s) and Mead and Blumer: we tie the theory’s foundation to Mead’s thought, but the name was given by Blumer six years after Mead’s death. Parsons and Merton get confused too: the AGIL scheme is Parsons’s, the manifest/latent function distinction Merton’s.

people-mead-notes.prompt: True or false: Mind, Self, and Society is the posthumous printing of a manuscript Mead had prepared before his death.
people-mead-notes.explain: False. The book was compiled by the editor Charles W. Morris mainly from student and stenographic notes of Mead’s lectures, plus some unpublished manuscripts. The mistake is natural: the author’s name is on the cover, but the book itself is a compilation, not an author’s book.

claim-two.prompt: Which of the following research questions is interactionist rather than functionalist?
options: How do news bulletins help society stay informed about dangers?
As a family watches the evening news, what do they say to each other and what meaning do they interpret the news with?
How does advertising revenue keep the media system going?
Which functional requirements of society does the media system meet?
claim-two.explain: The interactionist question looks at how people build meaning as they meet each other and something else; the second option asks exactly that. The other three options look at the system’s or society’s needs, contribution and continuity: these are functionalist questions.

con-agil.prompt: A university runs an orientation programme to teach new faculty members its academic values and traditions. Which AGIL letter does this job fall under?
options: A – Adaptation
G – Goal attainment
I – Integration
L – Latency (pattern maintenance)
con-agil.explain: Preserving values and motivation and passing them on to newcomers is the job of pattern maintenance (L). The most tempting wrong answer is “I”: orientation does bring people together, but I is about coordinating the parts and managing conflict; the real aim here is for values to pass from generation to generation. A concerns resources and adjusting to the environment, G setting goals and moving toward them.

con-merton.prompt: Imagine: a company bans social media use during working hours (aim: productivity). As a result employees start chatting face to face during lunch breaks and trust in the team grows; neither management intended this nor noticed it. In Merton’s language, what is this consequence?
options: A manifest function
A latent function
A dysfunction
A consequence irrelevant to the system (neither functional nor dysfunctional)
con-merton.explain: The consequence contributes to the system (the team), but nobody intended or noticed it: that is the definition of a latent function. A manifest function would have to be intended (the ban’s aim was productivity, not trust). It is not a dysfunction, because team cohesion is not weakened but increased. And it is not “irrelevant” either: the rise in trust touches how the team works.

con-looking.prompt: Imagine: after a presentation a student sees the teacher frown and thinks “I was awful”, while the teacher was actually thinking about a sore back. Which of Cooley’s three elements produces the student’s mortification?
options: What the teacher actually thinks
Imagining the teacher’s judgment of them
The real quality of the presentation
The mechanical reflection of the teacher’s facial expression, like a mirror
con-looking.explain: According to Cooley, what drives us is the imagined judgment: the student assumes the teacher holds a judgment of them. What the teacher really thinks (the first option) is out of play: the student does not know it. The fourth option is the most tempting, since the word “mirror” leads there; but Cooley says the opposite: what produces the feeling is not the mechanical reflection but the attributed sentiment.

con-mead-game.prompt: Imagine: a child playing “doctor” is a patient one minute and the doctor the next, ignoring turns and rules. Which of Mead’s stages does this correspond to?
options: Play (role-play)
The game (organised game)
Taking the attitude of the generalized other
The “I” stage
con-mead-game.explain: Arbitrary switching from role to role and the standpoint of one particular other are the marks of Mead’s play stage. In the organised game the child has to take into account, at the same time, everyone’s role on the team and how the roles relate (the baseball example). The generalized other is beyond even that: the standpoint of the organised community. The “I” belongs on a different axis, the spontaneity of the response.

con-mead-i-me.prompt: Imagine: a student who always stays quiet in class starts the discussion, to everyone’s surprise, and the next day says “how did I do that?”. In Mead’s framework, how is this surprise best explained?
options: Because the “me” produced a new generalized other.
The “I”’s response cannot be known in advance; the person sees it only afterwards, as a “me”.
Because the self consists only of the “me”, and the “me” behaves randomly.
Because the student has gone back from the organised game to the play stage.
con-mead-i-me.explain: Mead’s “I” is the response to organised expectations, and it cannot be known in advance; the person catches it only afterwards, in memory, as a “me”. The first option confuses the concepts: the “me” carries expectations, it does not produce a new other. The third makes the “me” random, when the “me” is the carrier of order. The fourth mixes developmental stages with the “I”/“me” distinction.

con-defsit.prompt: Imagine: a rumour spreads that “Bank X is failing”. The bank is in fact sound, but customers rush to withdraw their money and the bank really does get into trouble. How does Thomas’s sentence explain this?
options: The rumour was true; that is why the bank failed.
The rumour was false, but customers took the situation as real; their reactions produced real consequences.
The bank’s capital was inadequate anyway; the event was a coincidence.
The customers were passive; the outcome was the bank’s own decision.
con-defsit.explain: This is exactly what Thomas’s sentence says: even if the situation is not really so, if people define it so and act accordingly, the consequences are real. The first and third options assume the rumour was true or the bank was already in trouble; the scenario sets up the opposite. The fourth ignores the customers’ actions.

con-goffman.prompt: Imagine: a waiter jokes about customers as soon as he enters the kitchen and changes his expression as he steps out into the dining room. In Goffman’s language, what is the kitchen?
options: Front stage
Back stage
The generalized other
The looking-glass self
con-goffman.explain: The kitchen is where the audience (the customer) does not see, where the impression is prepared and the “dirty work” of the show is hidden: the back stage. The most tempting wrong answer is “front stage”: the waiter works there too, but the front stage is where the performance is given to the audience (the dining room). The generalized other and the looking-glass self are other theorists’ concepts and describe a mental process, not a place.

ass-blumer.prompt: Which of the following statements contradicts Blumer’s second premise?
options: The meaning of an advertisement takes shape together with the reactions of those who watch it.
The meaning of a symbol stays fixed in the object itself and is the same for everyone.
What friends say to each other affects what a song expresses.
The same word can carry different meanings in different communities.
ass-blumer.explain: The second premise says that meaning does not sit ready-made in the object but arises from interaction; the second option claims the opposite. The other three say that meaning is shaped by the community, by conversation and by context: in other words, they are consistent with the premise.

ass-func.prompt: True or false: Merton adopted as a principle the “indispensability” assumption often used by functionalists and rejected the idea of functional alternatives.
ass-func.explain: False; quite the opposite. Merton found the indispensability assumption debatable and put forward the concept of “functional alternatives”, which says the same need can be met by other structures too. This distinction opens the door both to the “whatever exists is justified” criticism and to debates about reform.

ass-micro-macro.prompt: Which of the following sentences stresses structure and almost ignores agency?
options: The audience reinterprets the message in light of their own experience.
Institutional structure is so determining that the audience’s choices hardly change the outcome.
Structures are produced by people’s actions and also limit those actions.
People can make choices even within the limits of institutions.
ass-micro-macro.explain: The second option reduces the individual’s choices to a detail that hardly changes the outcome, giving structure near-absolute determining power: it ignores agency. The first and fourth options stress the effect of agency. The third is close to Giddens’s “duality of structure”: it ties the two together and does not reduce one to the other.

how-func-steps.prompt: In the second step (“specify the unit”), why is it necessary to stop and ask “for whom?”
options: Because the same pattern can be functional for one subgroup and dysfunctional for another.
Because functions are defined only for individuals.
Because there is no such thing as a function at the level of society.
Because if this step is skipped, latent functions turn into manifest ones.
how-func-steps.explain: Merton’s emphasis is exactly this: a cultural item usually has both functional and dysfunctional consequences, and these fall differently on different units. The second and third options are wrong: functions can be defined for individuals, subgroups or the whole system. The fourth confuses the manifest/latent distinction with the unit.

how-lab.prompt: If in the first round of the exercise you write “the cinema gives young people a lesson in manners and dress that nobody intended”, which of Merton’s concepts does this correspond to?
options: Manifest function
Latent function
Dysfunction
The definition of the situation
how-lab.explain: A consequence that contributes to the system (young people’s socialisation) but was unintended and unrecognised: a latent function. A manifest function would mean the cinema was made and watched for that purpose. A dysfunction means harm; the sentence speaks of a contribution. “The definition of the situation” is Thomas’s concept and the subject of the interactionist round. (A reminder: this reading is our exercise; Blumer did not say so.)

evid-machine.prompt: In listing the political machine’s latent functions, what is Merton doing?
options: Defending the machine on moral grounds.
Looking at consequences beyond its stated purpose, and saying the machine will persist unless those needs are met in other ways.
Proving that all machines perform exactly the same functions.
Arguing that reform is unnecessary.
evid-machine.explain: Merton’s move is to understand why a condemned institution persists through its consequences, and to show that it will not go away unless other arrangements meet those needs. The first option is the most tempting wrong answer, but Merton states explicitly that he is not offering an apology. The third is wrong too: Merton does not claim that all machines perform the same functions to the same degree. The fourth is the opposite of what he wrote.

evid-payne.prompt: What is the limit of the “62 per cent imitation” finding in Blumer’s study?
options: It rests on people’s own written accounts; there is no control group and it does not prove that the cinema produced the imitation.
62 per cent is so high that it settles that the cinema produced the imitation.
It covers only factory workers.
Blumer never put the figure into numbers.
evid-payne.explain: The finding rests on people mentioning imitation in their own accounts, and Blumer’s own caution is that the counts should not be taken as conclusive. The second option mistakes a high percentage for proof of causation; that is a logical error. The third contradicts the sample (this figure comes from high-school students) and the fourth the numbers given in the text.

crit-fun.prompt: According to Merton’s 1949 answer, when does functional analysis risk sliding into a “conservative teleology”?
options: When it lists functions and dysfunctions together.
When it adopts the assumptions of functional unity, universal functionalism and indispensability without question.
When it separates manifest from latent functions.
When it searches for an institution’s alternatives.
crit-fun.explain: For Merton the criticism rests on these three assumptions: if everything is in harmony, every item is functional and every form is indispensable, there is no way left but to defend the existing order. The other three options are all tools Merton proposed to avoid this trap: seeing dysfunctions, separating latent functions, looking for alternatives.

crit-int.prompt: A researcher describes in fine detail how editors in a newsroom bargain over the meaning of a story, but never asks about the concentration of media ownership or the distribution of advertising revenue. Which criticism fits best?
options: The study is too quantitative; qualitative method should be dropped.
The study leaves social structure and power relations out.
The study depicts the individual as a passive puppet.
The study confuses manifest function with latent function.
crit-int.explain: The classic criticism of interactionism is that it describes micro detail skilfully while structure and power (here ownership and the revenue order) stay outside. The first option takes a qualitative study for a “quantitative” one. The third is the criticism directed at functionalism; and the manifest/latent distinction does not appear in this study at all.

today-func.prompt: A news app sends notifications constantly. Users read them, feel “I followed the agenda, I did my part”, and take none of the action the news called for. According to Lazarsfeld and Merton’s idea, how can this be read?
options: The app’s manifest function: getting the user to act.
A narcotizing dysfunction: an abundance of information takes the place of action.
Latent pattern maintenance: values passed from generation to generation.
The definition of the situation: the notification is a rumour.
today-func.explain: Settling for the information and not moving to action is the essence of the narcotizing dysfunction. (This is a reading, not an empirical claim.) The first option counts action as the manifest function, but in the scenario there is no action. The third is a concept from Parsons’s AGIL and has nothing to do with the topic. The fourth uses Thomas’s concept in the wrong place.

today-int.prompt: A user’s account is followed at the same time by family, colleagues and close friends, and because of this the user hesitates to make a joke. In Marwick and boyd’s language, what is this situation called?
options: Narcotizing dysfunction
Context collapse
Latent pattern maintenance
Play (role-play)
today-int.explain: Many different audiences gathered in a single context, forcing the user to adjust what they post, is “context collapse”. The narcotizing dysfunction is Lazarsfeld and Merton’s idea of media dysfunction; latent pattern maintenance is the L in Parsons’s AGIL; play is Mead’s childhood stage. None of them is the name of this situation.

today-lab.prompt: At what level does the “third question” at the end of the exercise show a question needs to be asked?
options: Micro level: the meaning of a conversation between two people.
Structural level: how do the platform’s design and business model bring audiences together?
Psychological level: how anxious is the student?
Historical level: how did people talk before social media?
today-lab.explain: The third question asks about the design and business model that determine the audience context: this is a structural-level question and fills the gap the two rounds left at the micro scale. The first option is already the subject of the interactionist round. The third and fourth options may be reasonable questions, but they are not the missing question this exercise points to.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question: “Which of the following matches is wrong?” Which is the correct answer?
options: Cooley: the looking-glass self
Mead: the generalized other
Cooley: the “I” and the “me”
Blumer: the person who coined “symbolic interactionism”
exam-patterns.explain: The “I” and the “me” are Mead’s concepts; Cooley’s concept is the looking-glass self. Exam writers often swap these two names. The other three matches are right: Cooley the looking-glass self, Mead the generalized other, and Blumer the person who introduced the term in 1937.

summary.prompt: True or false: for Merton a “latent function” is a secret aim hidden with bad intent.
summary.explain: False. For Merton a latent function is an unintended and unrecognised consequence, not a plan somebody conceals. Example: a ceremony may bring no rain and yet strengthen the community’s identity; none of the participants need have intended that consciously.

quiz.prompt: In Merton’s language, what does it mean for a consequence to be “latent”?
options: That it was concealed with bad intent
That it was unintended and unrecognised
That it is only negative
That it cannot be measured
quiz.explain: For Merton the latent is what was neither intended nor recognised. So it is not a secret plan (first option). A latent function is a positive consequence (that is, a function); if it were negative it would be called a latent dysfunction (the third option wipes out that difference). Measurability is a separate problem.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Blumer first used the term “symbolic interactionism” in his 1969 book.
quiz.explain: False. Blumer coined the term in 1937, in an essay in Man and Society, edited by Schmidt; the 1969 Symbolic Interactionism: Perspective and Method set the approach out at length. “1969” is a tempting wrong answer in exams, because the book’s title carries the term.

quiz.prompt: Match the books with their authors.
pairs: Human Nature and the Social Order
The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
quiz.explain: Mind, Self, and Society is known under Mead’s name but is a book compiled from student notes; Cooley’s book is Human Nature and the Social Order, written by his own hand in 1902. The Social System is Parsons’s, and the manifest/latent function distinction is in Merton’s Social Theory and Social Structure. Goffman’s book analyses everyday life in the language of theatre, and Blumer’s gathers interactionism into three premises.

quiz.prompt: Put the works and events in chronological order (oldest to newest).
items: Cooley: Human Nature and the Social Order (1902)
W. I. Thomas and D. S. Thomas: The Child in America (1928)
Merton: Social Theory and Social Structure (1949)
Blumer: Symbolic Interactionism: Perspective and Method (1969)
quiz.explain: The order is 1902, 1928, 1934, 1937, 1949, 1969. Points that get mixed up: Mead died in 1931, his book came out in 1934, after his death, and the term was coined in 1937; so the name comes after Mead’s book. Merton’s book came out in 1949 and Blumer’s systematic book on the approach in 1969.

quiz.text: In Parsons’s AGIL scheme, {{1}} describes the system securing resources from the environment, while {{2}} describes values and motivation being preserved and passed across generations.

options: adaptation
goal attainment
integration
integration
latency (pattern maintenance)
goal attainment

quiz.explain: Securing resources from the environment is adaptation (A); preserving and transmitting values is latency, or pattern maintenance (L). Integration (I) means harmony among the parts, and goal attainment (G) setting goals and directing resources to them; neither fits these definitions.

quiz.scenario: Imagine: a news site puts its comment section under strict moderation to reduce hate speech. A few months later readers start calling the site “censorious” on social media, and the site becomes the focus of that debate. Meanwhile, some of the former commenters set up a new community on another platform under their own pseudonyms and develop their own internal rules, jokes and a language that decides “who counts as respected”.

parts.prompt: The row over “censorship” is an unintended and unnoticed negative result of the moderation. In Merton’s language, what is it?
options: A manifest function
A latent function (positive contribution)
A latent dysfunction
parts.explain: The result is unintended and unrecognised (latent) and harms the system (dysfunction): a latent dysfunction. A manifest function would be intended; a latent function would be a positive contribution.

parts.prompt: The former commenters building their own language, rules and standards of reputation on the new platform is closer to the question of which view?
options: Functionalist: how the system meets its four requirements
Interactionist: how meanings and identities are built in interaction
Neither: it is a question of economics
parts.explain: The building of a shared language, rule and standard of respect within interaction is the subject of the interactionist view (meaning arises from interaction). A functionalist question can be asked too, but that view asks about contribution to the system; the interesting detail on the stage is how meaning is built.

parts.prompt: Which question in this event moves beyond the micro level to the structural level?
options: How does one commenter understand another’s joke?
In whose interest does the order of ownership and advertising revenue that sets comment policy operate?
What does a commenter take into account in choosing a pseudonym?
parts.explain: The order of ownership and revenue is an institutional structure outside interaction between individuals; this question is at the macro level. The other two are micro questions about how individuals build meaning and make choices.

quiz.takeaway: One event gives rise to two questions at once: the functionalist one, “what consequence did it have for the system?”, and the interactionist one, “how did people make sense of it and rebuild it?”; the structural question waits beyond both.

quiz.prompt: According to Mead, what is the “generalized other”?
options: A single adult a child imitates in role-play
The attitude of the organised community or social group that gives the individual a unity of self
The spontaneous, unpredictable response inside a person
A person’s imagining of how they look in other people’s eyes
quiz.explain: The generalized other is the standpoint of the organised community or social group as a whole. The first option describes the play stage, the third the “I”, and the fourth Cooley’s looking-glass self; they are all close but separate concepts.

quiz.prompt: True or false: in Goffman’s dramaturgy the back stage is where the impression is prepared and the everyday dirty work of the show is hidden.
quiz.explain: True. The front stage is the place of the official performance given to the audience; the back stage is that of preparation and what is hidden. A common mistake is to think of the back stage as “fake” and the front stage as “real”; Goffman treats both as parts of everyday life.

quiz.prompt: A researcher says “the media structure has such power that it leaves the audience’s interpretation almost indeterminate”. Which criticism fits best?
options: The study is buried too deep in micro detail.
The study puts structure first and ignores the role of the agent (the audience).
The study cannot separate manifest from latent function.
The study defines Mead’s “I” wrongly.
quiz.explain: The sentence gives structure near-absolute determining power and ignores the audience’s power to interpret and choose: in the structure–agency debate, the agent is forgotten. The first option says the opposite (being buried in micro detail is the language of a criticism aimed at interactionism). The third and fourth options are concepts that do not appear in the sentence.

quiz.prompt: Thomas’s sentence, “if men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences”, is the key idea of which view?
options: Structural functionalism: because it describes the system’s equilibrium.
Symbolic interactionism: because it ties behaviour to the meaning a situation has for people.
Both: because the two views say the same thing.
Neither: because the sentence has nothing to do with sociology.
quiz.explain: The sentence says that behaviour depends on the meaning a situation has for people; this is also consistent with Blumer’s first premise and is the core of the interactionist tradition. The functionalist question reads the event through the system’s need; the two views do not say the same thing, so the third option is wrong as well.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of the claim “Merton’s functionalism justifies whatever exists”?
options: True: because Merton said that every institution is indispensable.
Partly wrong: because Merton took dysfunctions and functional alternatives into account; but the criticism that the assumptions were misused in practice is not empty.
Entirely true: because Merton defended the political machine.
Entirely wrong: because no criticism was ever directed at functionalism.
quiz.explain: Merton took up the criticism himself and built dysfunctions and alternatives into the system; in his political-machine analysis he wrote that he was not offering an apology. But the frequent use of the three assumptions in the functionalist literature does not make the criticism void. So the second option is measured and correct; the other three are over-generalisations.

quiz.prompt: In the “micro–macro” distinction, how are functionalism and symbolic interactionism placed?
options: Both macro
Functionalism macro, interactionism micro
Functionalism micro, interactionism macro
Both micro
quiz.explain: Functionalism focuses on social systems and institutional structures, interactionism on interpersonal and interactional processes. The placement is a rough one: authors such as Fine argue that interactionism extends into macro areas too, and theorists such as Giddens discuss ways of linking the two levels.
